**Other emulators**
- **BlueStacks 5** runs x86_64 Android with GPU acceleration, and Termux runs on it, so our emulator build should install and run. Three catches:

- **Google Play Games for PC Developer Emulator** is Google's emulator built for testing games on PC. It has Vulkan and allows adb sideloading. Same install catch.
- MuMu Player, LDPlayer and Genymotion are similar. Windows Subsystem for Android is gone (Microsoft shut it down in March 2025).

**A real phone without adb**
- Copy the APK to your phone (cloud drive, email, USB file copy) and tap it to install. The app downloads everything itself, so adb is only needed to pull logs.

- Firebase Test Lab, AWS Device Farm and BrowserStack App Live rent you real Snapdragon phones you control remotely. They need an account, and most need payment after a free tier.

**ARM Android without a phone**
- An ARM cloud server (for example Oracle's free ARM tier) running Android in a container ("redroid") would test the phone build's ARM path end to end. There's no GPU there, so it would be slow.

Your phone's GPU driver then picked a compressed format, which the GPU can't draw into, so the atlas stayed empty and every icon came out black. The same failure hit a projectile/smoke texture. Compression is now always off. The emulator's driver never compresses these textures, which is why it never showed the bug.

**Lobby:** the lobby's "draw at full speed" setting is switched on once, on your next lobby start (60 fps instead of 30 while you're active). You can turn it back off in the lobby's Settings and it will stay off.

**Hardware cursor in the real game:** it's already on. Your phone's log shows BAR switching it on during the match, and the frozen-game test on the emulator showed the pointer still moving.

**Emulator vs. phone:** the emulator adds roughly 3–5 minutes per fix: an extra build, an install, and a slow game load at about 6 fps. It's only really needed for things I have to drive myself:
- **Multi-finger gestures:** I can't fake multi-finger touches on a phone that isn't rooted.
- **Your phone is in use:** it's locked, or you're playing on it.

For this fix I built only the phone version. Testing on your phone directly would be faster still, but it means I take over the phone while I test.

answer:
The profile found the real bottleneck, and it isn't BAR's graphics settings.

**What's happening:** the CPU and GPU take turns instead of working at the same time.
- **Main thread:** busy only about a third of each frame. For 43–58% of the frame it sits in the GPU driver, waiting for the GPU to finish.
- **GPU:** about 72% busy, but running at only 342–443 MHz of its 1200 MHz. The waits leave gaps, so the phone thinks the GPU isn't busy enough to speed up.
- **Ruled out:** Lua, the gamepad mod, proot and the worker threads are all small in this profile. That's why the Lowest preset barely helped.

**Why:** the graphics driver build we use fixed the black flickering by holding each frame until the GPU finishes it. That only overlaps CPU and GPU when the game has a third frame buffer, and the driver adds one only with vsync off. Our 30 fps cap is built on vsync, so the game is stuck with two buffers and keeps waiting.

**The test:** I've put a test switch on the phone that turns vsync off at the driver. It's a single file, `files/bar/dev-env.sh`, which I delete afterwards. It takes effect the next time BAR starts. Expect fps above 30 in light scenes during the test; it's uncapped for now.

If fps jumps in the same busy base, the fix is to keep vsync off and add our own 30 fps cap. That cap would pace the game without making the GPU wait, which should also let the GPU reach its full clock.

answer:
I found the cause of the frame-end wait. A fix is on your phone, but it's untested; I need you in a game to check it.

**Cause** (in the phone's graphics driver, lfdevs Mesa):
- The driver has two ways to hand a finished frame to the screen. In the efficient one, a helper thread waits for the graphics chip and the game keeps working. In the fallback, the game itself stops until the frame is fully drawn. That stop is the 42–51% wait we measured.
- The driver only uses the efficient way when it thinks the phone's kernel can't track frame completion on its own. Your Fold7's newer kernel says it can, but Qualcomm's graphics driver never feeds it that information. So every frame took the fallback and stalled.
- Your game had no helper thread, which confirms this.

**Fix:** our small library that already caps the frame rate now answers "not supported" to that one kernel query. The driver then switches to the efficient way. The X server part it needs is already in our build. If it misbehaves, a single setting (`BARDROID_PRESENT_FENCE=0`) turns it off.

**What it should change:** the processor and graphics chip can work at the same time instead of taking turns. The graphics chip should also look busier, so Android may raise its clock. The same scene should run noticeably faster, top-down and tilted.

**Risk:** the efficient way has never run on your phone before. If you see flicker, black frames or a freeze, tell me. Otherwise, once a busy game is on screen I'll check that the helper thread exists and the game has stopped waiting.

In big late games the phone is limited by the GPU, not the CPU: it runs 90–93% busy at its heat cap. So the remaining wins come from giving the GPU less to draw. Here's what's left, biggest first. I haven't changed or built anything yet.

I found three things the phone draws every frame for no visible result, and switched them off (commit 09e6e74). How much fps this gains is unmeasured, because the laptop's GPU behaves nothing like the phone's. It needs a late-game check on the phone.

**What was wasted:**
- **Map buffer pass:** BAR forces an extra off-screen buffer on (a "G-buffer", read by effects like lights). With your phone's Lowest preset, the engine only ever clears that buffer for the map, every frame, and nothing draws into it.
- **Trees and rocks drawn twice:** every tree and rock is drawn a second time into the matching buffer for models. What reads that buffer (lights, SSAO, bloom, distortion, outlines) is all off on the phone.
- **Fog-of-war stripes:** BAR's "Fog Diagonal Lines" effect runs a full-screen pass that finds the ground through that empty map buffer, so it discards every pixel and draws nothing on the phone.

**What changed:**
- **Touch widget:** turns off the map buffer pass while advanced map shading is off (it comes back if you turn shading on), and stops drawing trees and rocks twice. Units still go into the model buffer, so shields and the radar/jammer placement previews work as before.
- **Fog stripes:** switched off at game start while advanced map shading is off; BAR's default comes back when it's on.
- **Gamepad thread:** it no longer wakes 60 times a second when no pad is connected.

No visible change is expected. The touch widget test and all laptop checks pass.

**Ruled out:**
- **Other Lua code in big games:** I built a new profiler for the game's own scripts (`profile-big-game.ps1 -Gadgets`). On a 989-unit game they cost little: about 6 ms per second at normal speed and 0.19 ms per simulated frame. All Lua together is about 2% of the frame. The late game is still limited by the GPU, and catch-up by the simulation itself.
- **Settings BAR overrides:** the sound limit is reset to 128 by BAR's own options, and the Lua memory pools are turned off by the lobby's own settings.
- **BAR's GPU profiler:** it needs an engine feature that isn't in any released engine yet.

The laptop ran at about 6 fps all evening, even in a 2-unit skirmish, so its frame rates mean nothing today.

Not dumb at all. It's the right question, and it's partly possible. How much is possible depends on whether you're playing online or alone.

**What can be cut, with no change to the engine:**
- **Worker threads.** Part of the unit animation runs across several cores, so getting the thread count right can help. My 2 vs 4 test is running on the phone now.
- **Heat.** Once hot, the phone throttles the processor by temperature, so anything that makes less heat lets it run faster. That includes sound, a frame cap and less drawing.
- **BAR's Lua scripts.** On the laptop, switching off BAR's interface scripts cut simulation time by about a quarter. Trimming the costliest ones gets part of that back without losing the interface.

**What can only be cut with a different engine build:**

answer:
The ceiling is real, but the benchmark is worse than most real games: it puts 1,300 units into one fight on one spot from the start. In a real 8v8 the units are spread across the map and only part of them fight at once. So the first job is to find out how often real games hit the ceiling. Then we make the phone handle those moments gracefully.

**What happens when the phone hits the ceiling:** online games run in lockstep, so every player must compute every simulation tick. A phone that can't keep up falls a few seconds behind live play during the biggest fight and catches up when it calms down. Depending on how BAR's servers handle a lagging player, the game may slow down for everyone instead. We need to see which one BAR does.

**The plan, all online-safe:**
1. **Measure real games.** Play your own 8v8 replays (there are several in your BAR folder) on the hot phone at normal speed, with no drawing shortcuts. A replay runs exactly the same simulation as the live game, so it shows how far behind the phone falls in real late games and for how long. That gives us a real number to work towards.
2. **Battle mode.** When the simulation starts falling behind, the app automatically gives it the main thread: fps drops to about 15–20, and the engine skips drawing whatever it can until the game is caught up. The app already does this when you join a game in progress (the black "catching up" screen), so this extends existing code. You'd see lower fps in the worst fight instead of drifting behind the other players.
3. **Keep the phone cooler.** When hot, the processor is capped at 1.4 GHz; cooler, it reaches 2 GHz or more, so a cooler phone has about 30–40% more processor speed. The frame cap and resolution already cut GPU heat. The rest is physical: try a clip-on phone fan, and unplug the charger while playing. Only you can test those, but they may be the biggest single gain.
4. **Tonight's tests.** These cover whatever small online-safe settings are left, such as more worker threads.
5. **Later, if you want it:** offering engine fixes to BAR's engine team, such as the 7% animation fix, is the only way the simulation itself gets cheaper for everyone.

There's also a choice only you can make: if you host, BAR's lobby can cap the unit count for everyone in the game.

The replay benchmark would be quick to build (the benchmark tooling already exists) and could run on the phone tonight alongside the other tests.

answer:
No, group follow adds almost nothing.

- **Per frame:** it averages the positions of at most 40 units in the group, which costs a few hundredths of a millisecond, about 0.1% of a frame at 30 fps. I added the 40-unit cap because of your question, so huge groups can't make it more expensive.
- **Twice a second:** it works out which units belong to the group.
- **Camera movement:** the easing is the "smooth curve" you described. The camera speeds up and slows down gradually instead of jumping to each new spot, and that easing is only a few multiplications per frame.

Both pieces matter for smoothness. Easing alone would still give a small surge every half second, each time the group's centre was recalculated; with the centre moving every frame, the easing has nothing to jump.

Partly possible, but your test was right: in a busy late game the simulation is the limit, and lowering graphics doesn't speed it up.

**Why lowering graphics did nothing**
- **The game already protects the simulation.** The game engine runs the simulation and the drawing on the same processor thread. When the simulation falls behind, the engine keeps only 15% of that thread for drawing and lets the frame rate fall, down to 2 fps if it has to. That drop is the fps loss you saw.
- **BAR's presets mostly save graphics-chip work** (shadows, water, particles). The simulation's cost is untouched, and so are BAR's interface scripts, which run on that same thread. On the laptop profile the simulation took about half of that thread's time, BAR's scripts about a fifth and drawing only 13%.
- **Our measurements say the same thing:**
  - Your mid-game switch from medium to lowest in the 8v8 stayed at about 19 fps.
  - On the phone, 70% resolution gave no gain over 100% (game speed 0.89 against 0.95).

answer:
It's in between. Nothing is translated, but it isn't a native port either: the phone runs BAR's official Linux engine, inside a small Linux environment the app carries.

**What's native:**
- The engine is BAR's own Linux arm64 build. Its code runs directly on the phone's CPU at full speed. There is no x86 emulation of the kind Winlator or Box64 use.
- The graphics driver (Mesa's Freedreno) is an open-source driver for the Adreno GPU, so the phone's GPU draws the game's OpenGL directly.
- The game's Lua and BAR's content are exactly what the PC runs.

**What's the "wrapper":** the engine expects a Linux desktop, not Android, so the app provides one.
- **A Debian Linux userland (proot):** gives the engine the Linux files and libraries it expects. proot works by intercepting some of the engine's system calls, which is the main cost of this approach. Narrowing which calls it intercepts took the phone from 14 to 30 fps.
- **An X server inside the app:** gives the engine a desktop "window", which the app then shows on screen.
- **Audio:** passed from the engine's Linux audio output to Android's.

**Why not a full port:** a full port would rebuild the engine as a real Android app, with no container, no X server and Android's own graphics APIs. That needs engine changes, and online play needs BAR's official engine so every player's game stays in sync. Keeping the official binary is what makes online work today. A full port is what BAR's devs could do, and HELP-WANTED.md already names it as the next step ("an Android-native engine build (no proot, no X server)").

**What it means for speed:** the biggest late-game cost is the engine's own simulation, and that already runs natively. A full port would remove the proot and X server overhead, but how much that gains has never been measured.

Your Discord draft already describes it accurately ("official, unmodified Linux arm64 engine in a Debian container"). It doesn't use the word "port", but people will ask. Want me to add a line saying plainly that it isn't a native port yet?

Touch building is back and installed on your phone (commit 23c5e25). The laptop test passes all its checks. The taps and drags on the phone itself haven't been tested yet, so those are yours to try.

**How it works now**
- **Pick a building:** the build menu's page strip turns into **ONE · LINE · GRID · BORDER · ↻ · ✕** (picture above). The shape you chose is lit. There are no new panels.
- **Tap the map:** places one, and the building stays picked so you can keep placing.
- **Drag the map with LINE, GRID or BORDER:** builds a row, a filled area or a hollow ring. The app holds Shift (plus Alt or Ctrl) for the finger, so it's BAR's own line and area building, the same as with a mouse and keyboard.
- **Drag with ONE:** pans the map, as before.
- **↻** turns the building. **✕** or a long press puts it away.
- Every new building starts on ONE, so a drag never builds by surprise.

**Gamepad online: what the research found**
- **v0.8.5 can't run online as it is.** It depends on 10 changed BAR widgets, a network connection to the pad, and direct unit orders. Online, BAR loads its own unchanged widgets and blocks those things for user widgets.
- **What works today with nothing needed from BAR:** the pad acts as a mouse and keyboard to the game. The app already does this in the lobby; no widget, lobby setting or game rule can see or block it.

Fixed a bug where a gamepad that was connected but not being used kept dragging the pointer back to the middle of the screen (commit f7b5044). The new build is on your phone.

- **The bug:** while a pad is connected, the app checks it 60 times a second, even when you're not touching it. After every touch or mouse move, it pulled the pointer back to the centre. So with a pad connected, the pointer kept getting pulled away from your finger or mouse.

  - It also happened at the start of every game.
- **The fix:** the pointer only goes back to the middle once you actually use the pad again (a button, a stick or a trigger). If you touch the screen while it's already gliding back, the glide stops.

answer:
Recap since your "Do not stop until we get 30fps 8v8" (≈00:45):

**Where it stands (dev phone, late 8v8 at 20:00–22:30, 3,200–3,500 units, phone hot):**
- **21–22 → 25 fps at the 30 cap (26–27 uncapped), game speed x1.00, 0 desyncs in every run.** Not locked 30 yet: frames sit just over the 33 ms budget.
- These numbers are at **30% render scale (9% of the pixels)** to isolate the CPU, as you suggested. At 100% it was 11–15 fps; the GPU side comes after the CPU side reaches 30.
- 1% resolution crashes BAR's UI load (200×93 pixels gives NaN sizes, then a segfault), so 30% is the floor.

**Engine-branch changes (all sync-exact, each committed):**
- **Deferred present: the biggest win (+4–5 fps).** The main thread used to wait ~7 ms every frame for Mesa's driver thread. Now the frame is handed over after the next sim step, so that wait is gone.
- Unit LOS checks and the per-frame transform saves for units and features now run on all cores.
- Parallel loops are split finer, so the main thread waits less on slow cores.
- New setting that skips loading chosen visual-only gadgets (nano particles, fire/smoke, beam lasers…) in the unsynced half only.
- Profiler timers per Lua call-in and per widget/gadget, plus a fix for a BAR engine bug: `Spring.GetProfilerTimeRecord` failed on every call.

**Settings cuts tested:**
- MaxSounds 16, icons sooner, lower ground and tree detail, water off, fewer particles, all 8 cores.
- The units' second (G-buffer) draw pass turned off.
- Cosmetic widgets off: defense ranges, sensor circles, ally cursors, name tags. These change what you see, so they're your call before shipping.

**Ruled out (no gain):** Mesa GL thread, pinning threads to cores, hiding the whole UI, all-icon units.

**Found:**
- Sim alone takes ~13–15 ms of the 33 ms budget, and heat caps the prime core at 1.5–2.0 of 3.36 GHz.
- The 30 cap was wasting ~7 ms a frame: after any late frame the next one runs two sim steps and misses its slot too.

**Running now:** a fix that runs at most one sim step per drawn frame while the game is nearly caught up. My first version stalled the replay's fast-forward, so it's rebuilt and on the phone again.

**Other:**
- One GPU-driver hang ("Resource deadlock avoided"), the same failure seen twice before these changes. The test tool now detects hangs.
- Loop item done: the Free memory button now has a pressed look (committed 33e1d00).
- Nothing pushed; the Fold7 wasn't touched.

answer:
AIRDROP TO PHONE now works on whatever Wi-Fi the laptop is on. Nothing depends on the home network's addresses: the laptop recognizes the Fold7 by its pairing key and searches for it each time. I could only test on the home Wi-Fi tonight.

**How it finds the phone** (a few seconds at most):
1. A USB cable, if the phone is plugged in. It's the fastest route and needs no network.
2. The phone's last address, and the laptop's gateway. On the phone's hotspot or USB tethering the phone *is* the gateway, so it's found at once.
3. Where adb sees the phone, through adb's mDNS. This follows the wireless debugging port when it changes.
4. A scan of the laptop's current subnet, up to 4094 addresses; on bigger networks, the laptop's own /24.
5. Tailscale.

**Tested** with no remembered address: found in 2.1 s. The gateway, adb and scan steps each work on their own.

**Re-pairing is never needed.** The app's pairing doesn't depend on the network. On the Fold7, Android keeps the laptop's adb key (`kaili@KAILILLAPTOP`) across networks. But wireless debugging only turns itself back on on trusted networks ([private], [private] 5G, CXNK01451709); on any other Wi-Fi it needs one tap on the phone. The tool doesn't need adb for sending, so this only matters for the adb helpers.

**When the phone can't be reached**, the notice says why within about 8 s instead of hanging (checked on screen):
- "This laptop is not on a network"
- "Fold7 not found on <Wi-Fi>"
- "<Wi-Fi> keeps devices apart": the phone is on the network but it blocks device-to-device traffic, as hotel and public Wi-Fi often do.

Each message suggests the phone's hotspot or a USB cable. The files wait meanwhile and go out by themselves once the phone is reachable.

**Fallbacks**
- **Phone's hotspot:** join it from the laptop. It's one Wi-Fi hop, so it's fast, and the tool finds the phone instantly as the gateway.
- **USB cable:** used automatically whenever plugged in.

**mDNS (finding the phone by name)**
- **Partly unavailable:** the Fold7 ignores mDNS queries while it sleeps.
- **Its announcements do reach the laptop:** it sends one when it joins a network, and I added one when its screen turns on.
- **But Windows Firewall blocks the tool from receiving them.** The first time it listened, Windows created Block rules and showed a "Windows Security" prompt, which is probably still open on the laptop. I didn't change the firewall.
- **For now, mDNS stays off by itself and everything else works,** because transfers only go out from the laptop.

**Speed, 295 MB test video**
- **Direct link:** 19.0–22.2 MB/s (13 s) when the Wi-Fi was quiet; 10.5–11.9 MB/s at its busiest.
- **adb push, same minutes:** 11.2 MB/s and 6.8 MB/s, so the direct link is about twice as fast.

I deleted my extra test copies from the phone; Download still holds the one test video and photo from earlier.

Decisions for you:
- **Firewall prompt:** allow "AIRDROP TO PHONE" on Private networks if you want the tool to also find the phone by name on big networks. It's optional. You can change it later under Windows Security › Firewall & network protection › Allow an app through firewall.
- **Keybind:** keep Ctrl+Shift+A in File Explorer, or name another key or a mouse side button.

answer:
I built the AirDrop-style Wi-Fi Direct link and it's installed on both sides. It works with no dialogs, but it doesn't reach "ultra" speed on this hardware, because the laptop's single Wi-Fi radio has to share time between your home Wi-Fi and the direct link.

**How it works:** the phone app finds the laptop over Wi-Fi Direct and connects. The laptop accepts in code and runs the link next to its normal Wi-Fi. Neither side shows a dialog, and the encrypted, pinned connection runs on top. Setup takes 5–10 s. The first time, Windows lists the Fold7 as a paired Wi-Fi Direct device.

**Where it helps — when there's no usable shared network:**
- **When:** for example hotel Wi-Fi that blocks devices from seeing each other, or no common Wi-Fi at all.
- **What happens:** while the phone can't be reached, the laptop makes itself visible on Wi-Fi Direct, and sharing on the phone goes straight to it.
- **Tested:** I made the phone refuse every other connection and shared the 295 MB video. It arrived in 15 s (**19.4 MB/s**), 24 s from share to saved, and was sorted into `Videos › From Fold7` as usual.

**Why it isn't "ultra" at home:**
- **Same channel:** Windows always runs the direct link itself, on the same channel as your home Wi-Fi (5220 MHz), so the radio takes turns between the two.
- **Speeds:** the direct link did 19–34 MB/s, the router path 25–34 MB/s with your phone near the router.
- **Both paths at once:** a 1.18 GB file using both did 21.8 MB/s, against 22.9 MB/s router-only.
- **Setup cost:** setting the link up also slows the home Wi-Fi for those 5–10 s while it scans.

So on home Wi-Fi, a big transfer only brings the direct link in when the router path is slow: under 15 MB/s after 3 s, with more than ~20 s left, for example with the phone far from the router. Then both paths carry the file. You can change this in `config.txt` (`WifiDirect`, `WifiDirectFromMB`, `WifiDirectBelowMBps`).

**Hotspots:**
- **Laptop's hotspot:** it runs on that same Wi-Fi Direct adapter and channel, so it would hit the same limit. It's also a Windows setting I'd leave to you.
- **Phone's hotspot:** this could be genuinely faster, but only if the laptop leaves your home Wi-Fi for the length of the transfer. That cuts its internet, including this Remote Control session.

**Truly fastest today:** a USB cable. The tool already uses it first whenever the phone is plugged in; I haven't measured it since the Fold7 is wireless-only right now. An Ethernet cable from the laptop to the router would also help.

**Fixed along the way:**
- When the Wi-Fi Direct adapter came up, the laptop used to treat it as a network change and drop its watch connection to the phone; that no longer happens.
- A block resent after a broken connection is now counted only once.

Yes, the laptop's hotspot would keep the laptop on home Wi-Fi, but it wouldn't be a turbo mode. It would run exactly like the Wi-Fi Direct link the tool already has, at the same speed, so there's nothing extra worth building. I didn't change anything.

Windows' Mobile Hotspot is a Wi-Fi Direct group under a different name: the card reports "Wi-Fi Direct GO: Supported" and "P2P Max Mobile AP Clients: 8". It's the same thing the tool now sets up itself, without touching your Windows settings.

Your card has one radio, so anything it runs next to home Wi-Fi has to sit on the home Wi-Fi's channel (5220 MHz) and take turns with it. That's why the direct link measured 19–34 MB/s against 25–34 MB/s through the router.

The phone's hotspot can't be the turbo either: the card reports "Maximum Number of Secondary STAs Supported: 0", meaning it can't join a second Wi-Fi network while it's on yours. It would have to leave home Wi-Fi, which you don't want.

On the phone side, the tool already does the "both at once" version: it joins the laptop's direct link as a Wi-Fi Direct client and stays on home Wi-Fi. A normal hotspot join would knock it off home Wi-Fi too.

So with both connections kept, about 30 MB/s is this laptop's ceiling over the air. For more, the options are:
- **USB cable:** used automatically whenever the Fold7 is plugged in; much faster, though I haven't measured it yet.
- **Ethernet:** the laptop on a cable to the router, so the router path is one Wi-Fi hop instead of two.
- **Different hardware:** a Wi-Fi card with two radios.

The Wi-Fi Direct link stays as it is: it steps in when the phone can't be reached over any network, or when the router path is slow.

answer:
Yes, it's not too complicated, and it barely costs any battery, because the base for it is already on your devices. Tailscale is on your laptop, your Fold7 and one more device in your Tailscale network (maybe the desktop). AIRDROP already accepts Tailscale addresses and remembers each device's Tailscale address.

**Why it doesn't work yet from outside:** Tailscale on your Fold7 is set to route only some apps, and AIRDROP isn't one of them. That's why your laptop couldn't reach AIRDROP on the Fold7 over Tailscale just now (no answer in 4 s). Fix: Tailscale app → Settings → split tunneling (its app list) → add AIRDROP. That's a setting on your phone, so it's yours to change.

**Security:** Tailscale is WireGuard, already encrypted end to end. AIRDROP's own family encryption still runs inside it, so only family devices can connect even there.

**Speed:** Tailscale tries a direct device-to-device connection. Away from home, speed is limited by the sender's upload: your home upload or the phone's mobile-data uplink, roughly 1–10 MB/s. If carrier networks block a direct path, Tailscale relays the traffic, which is slower. I can't measure any of this while both devices sit on your home Wi-Fi.

**Battery and data:** Tailscale already runs on your phone, so AIRDROP adds almost nothing. The one cost: computers keep a connection to each phone and ping it every 3 minutes. On mobile data, each ping wakes the cellular radio. I'd change three things:
1. **No pings over mobile data.** Computers stop keeping that connection while a phone is on mobile data. The phone sends straight to the computer when you share, and checks who's online only when you open the app or the share panel.
2. **Ask before large files on mobile data.** Above about 100 MB it would ask "Send now over mobile data" or "Wait for Wi-Fi".

answer:
Not the way you describe, but a radical rewrite that keeps the numbers identical is feasible, and three agents are now working on it.

**Why not a cheaper approximate simulation or a spoofed sync:** BAR multiplayer is lockstep. Every player's device runs the whole simulation, and only orders travel over the network. If the phone computed even slightly different numbers, it wouldn't just raise a warning. Your phone would quietly play a different game from everyone else (units in different places, fights ending differently), and faking the "in sync" signal only hides that. It's also the one condition BAR's devs set for a patched engine: the synced simulation stays identical.

**What's running now:** three background agents, each rewriting one of the most expensive simulation areas to produce exactly the same numbers much faster. They're using leaner data layouts, fewer memory allocations, more work spread across the phone's cores, and vector math that rounds exactly like the original.
- **sim-lua:** BAR's Lua interpreter, 23 % of the main thread.
- **sim-move:** unit movement and collision, the simulation's largest part.
- **sim-units:** unit scripts, weapons and line of sight.

Each keeps a change only if it passes the full 8v8 replay with 0 desyncs and measures faster. They share the dev phone through the queue, never touch your Fold7, and push nothing. My honest expectation is 20–40 % off those parts over many hours of work, not "almost no cost". Nothing has come back from them yet.

**The only path to near-zero simulation cost** is the phone not running it at all: another machine runs the real simulation and the phone draws the game and sends your orders.

Automatic updates now work with no GitHub. Your Fold7 installed update 29 by itself 15 seconds after I published it.

**How it works:**
- `Publish Update.bat` on your laptop builds AIRDROP for computers and phones and signs it with a release key. That key exists only on your laptop, in `state\release-key.dat`.
- Your laptop tells every device it can reach within 10 seconds. Each device downloads the update, checks the signature and installs it right away, as you asked. The only exception: a file transfer running at that moment holds it back a few seconds.
- Devices also pass the update on to each other, so one that was away from your laptop still gets it from another device.
- A device takes only updates signed with your laptop's key. Not even a stolen family phone can push a program onto the others.

**Tested on your devices:**
- Fold7: installed updates 27, 28 and 29 on its own, with no tap needed.
- Laptop: replaced its own program and restarted in about 3 seconds.
